title: Battling AI fatigue as a designer and developer: a practical guide
text:
Battling AI fatigue as a designer and developer: a practical guide

AI is great, but it doesn’t have to take over your life

A warning about using AI for everything

Not too long ago, I needed a new app for writing down my expenses so I could better keep track of my money, so I searched the iOS App Store.
I found many apps for expense reports, for budgeting and money management in general, but something felt strange. As a UI Designer and a Front-end Developer, I can spot patterns in the designs, and these apps weren’t human-made.

Most of the apps I found were AI-generated, vibe-coded apps, and I didn’t really want to use any of them, so I decided to make my own expenses app.
I fired up Claude Code in my terminal and started making a web app, this web app I opened in Safari on iOS, and from there I used the “Add to Home Screen” feature to use it like a native iOS app, more or less.

I’m no stranger to Claude Code, I vibe coded apps and websites before — both for work and personal use, but this time it felt different.
At work I use AI all day every day, I code websites with Claude Code, I also generate designs in Figma using the same AI, I often draft emails and make them sound more robust or more professional with an AI assistant, sometimes I even let the AI draft the email itself.

Some of the projects I do are generated in Figma using AI prompts, then they are coded from the generated designs in Figma into real websites, using AI as well, and at the end they are sent to the client with a professional-sounding AI-generated email message with the live website link, AI did all the actual work.

This AI-based workflow I’m describing isn’t rare these days.

This AI-based workflow I’m describing isn’t rare these days, lots of people use AI for everything and Front-end development is often cited as the industry most disrupted by AI usage.

Still, I think that was why it felt strange using AI to vibe-code my personal expenses web app in my free time, I was offloading my free time into an AI workflow as well.

I realized this was a sign of “AI fatigue” as it is now known in the industry, and I found a few ways to make it better so I decided to share them in this article.

Try to limit your usage of AI

Not every task should go through ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or your AI assistant of choice. Even if this task could be done quicker, there is a sense of accomplishment in doing things on your own. To start with, I would recommend that if you use AI heavily at work, try to avoid using it in your personal life.

If you plan a vacation, you can plan it yourself like you used to do a decade ago, by searching Google and asking friends for recommendations. Will you miss some attractions? Possibly. Will it matter in the long run? Probably not.

It’s worth it if it gets you out of the AI mindscape that leaves you a mere participant in your own life; if it’s only in your work life, it will feel much more manageable.

As Tyler Durden told us in “Fight Club” (1999), “You are not your job” (see image above), if your job requires you to use a certain technology — it doesn’t mean YOU need to use it, only your office persona needs to. Your free time is your own.

Do the fun parts yourself

I know this part might be controversial, but small and easy tasks you can do yourself in the same amount of time as the AI — you SHOULD do yourself. Not only that, you should also do the fun parts yourself, instead of asking AI to assist, even if it means it will take longer to complete, because the fun part is for you, the AI won’t have fun for you.

Finding out what you feel is the fun part is subjective and everyone will have fun with different parts, some coders like the math of it all, some like to build the UI, I like to hand code the CSS animations, so I’m not asking the AI to do THAT part for me. I will animate it myself.

Also, I don’t ask the AI to write for me. Ever. Not this article, no WhatsApp, no Slack messages, nothing. If I send something into the world, I wrote it myself.

For me writing is thinking and I don’t want to outsource it to a machine.

I might consult the AI about the writing process, I might ask it for information, or a summary, for its opinion on my writing, but the writing itself is my own, the thinking behind it is my own, and the final decision on what to change is also my own. For me, writing is thinking, and I don’t want to outsource it to a machine, at least not yet.

Don’t be 100x more productive

If you’re using AI in your workflow to be more productive, you’re probably already between 5x to 10x more productive than you used to be. Trying to maximize this and become 100x more productive will lead you to obsession and self burnout, please don’t do that to yourself.

invest in work quality, not quantity.

I know it’s very tempting, you tell yourself you can make an entire year’s work in a week, or even less but please realize that work is endless, you will never get everything done, work will always fill more of your time. Beware of productivity paradoxes.
A better way is to stay 10x more productive and just work happier, not harder, not longer, just make work more satisfying, invest in work quality, not quantity.

Invest in the work itself and not in the pipeline that made you get there because no pipeline will work 100% of the time and you’ll get crazier and crazier trying to perfect the pipeline using new models, new apps or new methods, instead of perfecting the work that you do with the help of your AI pipeline.

You are not staying behind

Tech people will always tell you that you HAVE to use any new technology, or else you’ll be left behind, you’ll become irrelevant in the near future.
Let me tell you right now — you’re NOT staying behind by NOT trying any new AI assistant, any new coding app or by not using the newest models.

Whenever something becomes essential for your job, you will learn it then. You don’t need to prepare yourself in advance by knowing all the digital tools in existence like you’re preparing for the digital apocalypse. Tools will come and go and they rarely matter in the great scheme of things.

You don’t need to prepare yourself in advance by knowing all the digital tools in existence like you’re preparing for the digital apocalypse.

Let me give you an example from my own job history, I remember when Sketch first came out, it was a UI Design software that was built from the ground up for UI Designers, any design software before it was a general purpose tool like Adobe’s Illustrator or Photoshop.

Many of my friends jumped on it, learning it early on and working with it as much as they could on their own jobs, trying to convince their managers to invest in a new design tool and blazing new workflows for it.

I didn’t do that, since Sketch was Mac-only and I was on Windows pre-2020 I waited, still using Adobe’s apps in the meantime. A couple of years later Figma came along (and won the UI Design software game).

I of course learned Figma but by not learning Sketch I was less tired of design tools compared to most of my peers, I managed to become a Figma expert much quicker and I didn’t need to convince my managers to abandon Adobe-based workflows as many already abandoned them for Sketch a year or two before.

Most of the times picking the winning technology, once it becomes clear, will be a much better strategy than learning all the new tools thinking you’ll otherwise be left behind. You’ll just tire yourself of technology all together.

Conclusion

Feeling fatigued about AI is natural, as it seems AI has completely taken over every aspect of our lives, but here in this article I outlined some key points that worked for me.

Leaving the AI at work feels liberating, it felt like in the early 2000s we left the internet at our home computers and never thought about it until we got back home.

Also letting go of some misconceptions I had about being 100x more productive, or about being left behind, which are ideas you hear all the time, either from your peers or from social media but aren’t in any way grounded in reality.

Ironically enough — my expenses app, froggo, that started all of this and made me write this article, is still an app I use every day to track my money and it earned its spot on my iPhone’s home screen.

Those are some of the tips that worked for me, but I saw many more tips online when I was doing research for this article, and I’m sure many people have their own strategies.

If you find something that worked for you and can also work for others, please leave it as a comment, I read all the comments and I can’t wait to see what worked for other humans.

And remember, AI usage can really affect your mood, so use it wisely.
Thanks for reading to the end 🙏

Further Reading

Beware of Productivity Paradoxes / Cal Newport

AI Fatigue is Real and Nobody Talks About It / Siddhant Khare

How I Broke Free from AI Fatigue / Kessie — Elevate Squad

How AI is quietly exhausting you — and what to do about it / Fast Company

What to do against AI Fatigue in your company? / Geoffroy de Lestrange

AI Fatigue Is Real — You’re Not Behind, Just Overstimulated / Tajinder Singh

Artificial Intelligence and Giving Up on Life / Robin VanGilder

title: The UX of Contrast: Lessons from Indika’s Game Design
text:
The UX of Contrast: Lessons from Indika’s Game Design

Introducing PX Contrast: a deliberate layering of conflicting player experiences leading to intentional multiple interpretations

Contrast is one of the most familiar visual tools for guiding attention in design. But in Indika it becomes a game UX tool. It shapes how players interpret the story. Released in 2024 by Odd Meter, the game won Best Narrative at the Games for Change Awards 2025 for its unconventional storytelling.

I first played Indika on release, and one thing kept bothering me: why do different parts of the experience look like they belong to completely different games? Its gameplay, sound, progression, and UI constantly pull against player expectations, yet together they express the same emotional conflict.

I call this approach Player Experience Contrast (PX Contrast): a sustained state where conflicting player experiences coexist, allowing players to hold different interpretations of the same interaction at once.

https://medium.com/media/2a925068042b626efe9447adfeba287f/href

A nun, a Devil, and a World that Stops Making Sense

You play as Indika, a young Orthodox nun who moves from complete obedience to rejecting her faith entirely. She carries the Devil with her, quite literally, inside her head, as she searches for identity outside the monastery walls. He whispers things Indika would never dare to say out loud, and raises questions she initially experiences as sinful. As the game progresses, the line between his voice and her own becomes increasingly blurred.

That internal split shows up in the world around her, too. At first, Indika feels surprisingly grounded. The game opens in a monastery that looks entirely believable. Growing up in Russia, I immediately recognized the monastery’s visual language, and that familiarity made the later transformation of the world feel even more unsettling.

As the game progresses, that realism breaks down the same way Indika’s certainty does. Historical accuracy gives way to dream logic: a cow the size of a barn, steam-powered machinery, ginormous bells, and many other bizarre things. The further you go, the less “real” the world becomes and the less sure Indika is of what she believes.

The world she discovers can only be described as a wild combination of comedy and tragedy straight out of the novels by Dostoyevski and Bulhakov.
— From the game’s official Steam page

That description captures the game’s tone remarkably well. It swings constantly between dark comedy and genuine dread, wrapping its story in symbolism and dream logic. Even the name “Indika” feels deliberate. Its resemblance to Cannabis indica adds another possible layer of meaning, especially given the game’s recurring themes of altered perception and reality.

That symbolism also reflects creator Dmitry Svetlov’s own experience. In an interview with The Guardian, he described growing up religious before becoming an atheist. Rather than criticizing faith itself, the game explores the broader system of beliefs and values that shapes a person’s identity.

Like any strong symbolic work, it invites multiple interpretations. What follows is my reading of the game and the role I believe its game UX design plays in supporting it.

Defining PX Contrast: Three Conditions for Meaningful Contradiction

PX Contrast builds on existing discussions of contrast in game UX (e.g., Salama’s Affinity vs Contrast framework), but extends the concept beyond momentary friction or immersion-breaking elements that pull players out of the experience.

PX Contrast is a deliberate layering of conflicting player experiences that coexist without resolution, allowing players to hold multiple interpretations of the same interaction simultaneously.

The term contrast here does not simply mean visual difference or opposing elements placed next to each other. In PX Contrast, the difference between systems creates a contradiction in how the player interprets the experience and feels the tension.

PX Contrast works when three conditions are met:

  1. Two or more systems (interface, sound, pacing, progression, environment, and others) create different interpretations of the same experience, allowing contrasting meanings to coexist.
  2. The contrast between these elements serves the same underlying theme, rather than existing as a purely aesthetic or mechanical choice.
  3. The contrast is intentional. It is a deliberate design choice that supports the player’s interpretation, rather than an unresolved inconsistency.

PX Contrast vs. Ludonarrative Dissonance

The other closely related term is ludonarrative dissonance, coined by Clint Hocking in 2007, describing moments when a game’s story and its mechanics pull in different directions. Since then, some designers and critics have started treating it as a deliberate tool rather than something to avoid. Connor Jackson, for instance, has argued for moving away from Hocking’s framing of the concept as a flaw, toward seeing it as a meaningful expressive device.

Dissonance describes the player’s feeling of mismatch, while PX Contrast describes the design structure that creates that tension. Not just gameplay versus narrative, but interface, sound, pacing, progression, and environment all contributing to the same emotional tension.

How Indika Uses PX Contrast

In Indika, the player and the protagonist share the same fractured perception: sacred rituals collide with gamified mechanics, slow reality with fast memories, and distorted spaces with normal ones. Neither side wins, creating a sustained tension that mirrors Indika’s inability to resolve her faith.

As a case study of PX Contrast, the game’s interface, pacing, and sound each pull against player expectations in different ways. Yet rather than creating noise, these сonflicting systems converge to teach players how to see the world through Indika’s broken perspective.

1. The Interface: Turning Faith Into Feedback

What also caught my attention was how the interface itself became part of the storytelling and how it shaped the way I experienced the main character’s journey. Rather than supporting the fiction of the world, it creates distance from it, aligning the player’s perspective with Indika’s own experience.

The interface gradually reshapes player expectations: actions that should feel sacred are reframed as ordinary gameplay interactions. That mirrors Indika’s own emotional detachment from her faith (she “plays” rather than truly believes). Religious rituals have stopped meaning anything. They’re just points in a mind game now. The interface teaches players to hold sacred and gamified readings at once without choosing.

This interpretation is also reflected in Svetlov’s own words:

The Game became a very important metaphor for our story. The game we all play, according to rules we didn’t make up, waiting for the reward that’s destined for us in case of “victory,” and living in fear of punishment in case of “defeat.”
— Dmitry Svetlov for Game Developer
https://medium.com/media/8b66af106072fe210230da9a71869fd8/href

One question the game raises from a design perspective is whether this spacial UI elements appearing near the character is deliberately non-diegetic (visible only to the player, not part of the game world), or whether Indika can actually perceive these game interface elements as part of her own mental reality.

I don’t think the game provides a definitive answer, and that’s what makes the question so interesting. Both interpretations contribute to PX Contrast, expanding the storytelling through intentional design.

  • If the UI exists only for the player, it creates distance between the player and the world.
  • If Indika can see it too, the interface becomes another expression of her fractured perception, extending the idea that the world we experience is shaped by her state of mind.

The game’s mechanics contradict the meaning these rituals appear to have within the world. Lighting candles and praying are not presented as moments of spiritual reflection, but as actions that generate points and rewards.

Normally, this gap between gameplay and narrative would be considered a design inconsistency. Here, the inconsistency becomes intentional feedback about the character’s internal conflict.

2. Sound: When a Prayer Sounds Like a Reward

Sound in Indika runs on the same contrast logic as the UI, and it’s easiest to see when you break it into a sequence:

  1. What the player does
  2. What they expect to hear
  3. What they actually hear
  4. What that mismatch makes them feel

Indika lights a candle and prays. The action carries the weight of a real religious ritual, so the player naturally expects silence, reverence, or something restrained. Instead, the game answers with a bright, cheerful retro chime. The kind of sound that says “you did it” in Duolingo, not “you were heard” in a church.

The brain reads it as a small reward, a completed task. That reading collides directly with the religious meaning of the action itself, and the player is left holding both interpretations at once. It’s the same dissonance Indika feels toward her own faith: the gesture is still performed, but the meaning behind it has quietly drained away.

Instead of reinforcing the atmosphere traditionally, the sound design creates intentional friction between action feedback and emotional context. Sacred and unsettling sounds exist alongside cheerful game-like effects and UI, forcing the player to question how these elements can belong to the same experience.

https://medium.com/media/aa38bef22ee08ced3d3020403523c590/href

3. Pacing: Slow Devotion vs. Fast Memory

In the “real” game world, movement is slow and heavy. One of the first tasks, carrying buckets of water, takes real time and effort, which reinforces just how monotonous monastic life is.

In the “real” game world, movement is slow and heavy. One of the first tasks, carrying buckets of water, takes real time and effort, which reinforces just how monotonous monastic life is. The platformer sections inside Indika’s memories are the opposite: fast, reactive, and sometimes genuinely tense. That tonal shift in pacing is another strand of the same contrast running through the whole game.

In the racing section, the contrast between the “real” world and Indika’s memories becomes even more explicit. Indika asks how to control the vehicle, and the answer comes through literal button instructions embedded in the dialogue between the characters (not through the usual on-screen control prompt). The game’s rules for the player become part of the rules governing Indika’s own memory, blurring the boundary between the player’s reality and hers.

https://medium.com/media/8616099f5a80911a2fb278f612fd77ca/href

As the Devil’s influence grows, his voice becomes more persistent and the boundary between realities begins to collapse. The screen floods with red, the music intensifies, and his voice merges with distorted sounds, overwhelming Indika’s own presence. Then a short prayer pulls her back into “normal” reality: the colors return, the Devil’s voice disappears, but a low, muffled sound remains underneath.

Switching between these states turns contrast into a gameplay system: players learn to interpret changes in visuals, sound, and control as signals of Indika’s mental state.

https://medium.com/media/abaae94df2e6b91bff2325e6e0c152f1/href

4. The illusion of Progression

Like the rest of Indika’s design, the progression system borrows the visual and sound design of retro games while quietly questioning the meaning behind it.

Mechanically, the player interacts with a familiar progression system: unlocking perks in a skill tree and collecting points. But all this progression exists only to generate more faith points. It becomes a reward loop without meaningful progression, exposing the emptiness behind the system. The accumulation of points feels as hollow as the rituals that produce them.

This idea reaches its peak at the end of the game: after everything Indika goes through, she finally receives an endless amount of points while trying to fulfill her wish. Yet the reward she spent the entire game chasing turns out to be completely meaningless.

https://medium.com/media/e402de0a5be3f22dbb76ca0af46ee044/href

Ironically, the faith points matter not because of what they unlock, but because of what they never do. Their mechanical emptiness mirrors the emotional emptiness Indika feels toward rituals she can no longer truly believe in.

And although technically it doesn’t change anything, all players continue to collect these points, including the developers. I think it can be viewed as a small social experiment.
— Dmitry Svetlov for Game Developer

5. Environment: From Order to Ruin

The contrast in Indika extends beyond individual mechanics into environmental storytelling. The game begins in a clean, organized monastery. Its architecture creates order and stability. By the end, this image is completely reversed: the player arrives in a broken and distorted landscape filled with ruined houses, dirty streets, and warped windows. The world itself reflects the uncertainty and conflict that have been growing throughout the game.

The environment becomes another feedback system: as the world grows more distorted, players learn to read the space itself as a signal of how far Indika’s grip on reality has slipped.

This change is reinforced through camera perspective. The final sequence shifts from third person to first person, placing the player inside an already distorted world. Combined with the warped camera angle this makes the experience feel more unsettling. The player is no longer just watching a broken world but experiencing it directly.

Core UX signal: this shift changes not just what the player sees, but how much control and orientation they feel they have.

By creating such a strong contrast between the beginning and the end, Indika leaves space for interpretation. The game does not give a simple answer about what is real, what is faith, or what is illusion. Instead, it places the player inside that uncertainty and lets them confront the same contradictions that define Indika’s journey.

Five Ways to Design with PX Contrast in Mind

Indika shows that effective game UX does not always require traditional consistency. Sometimes intentional inconsistency can create meaning. PX Contrast shows how contradictions between systems can become coherent when they reinforce the same emotional idea.

A few practical takeaways I’ll carry into my next project:

  • Start from the meaning, not the mismatch. Before introducing contrast between two systems, define what emotional or thematic idea it should express. Contrast that doesn’t serve a specific idea reads as inconsistency, not design.
  • Repeat the same idea across several systems. A single contradictory detail is easy to dismiss as a bug. PX Contrast works when multiple systems carry a version of the same idea through different means, so the pattern becomes unmistakably intentional. Consistency of intent is what separates PX Contrast from ludonarrative dissonance.
  • Let one system contradict another to hold two readings at once. For example, the visuals may suggest one meaning while sound or controls suggest another. Neither has to be “correct.” The player holds both interpretations at once and that unresolved tension is what PX Contrast is designed to create.

Why it still stays with me

None of this requires knowing what Svetlov actually intended. Games, like any art form, keep generating interpretations their creators never planned for. The strongest ones leave room for that. Indika did that for me. I played it in 2024, and it still stays with me because every part of its design serves the same emotional truth: it creates contrast without trying to resolve it.

After all, we so often look for simple answers in art and so often remain dissatisfied when we’re left alone with uncomfortable unanswered questions. But isn’t that the best thing that any experience can give us?
— Dmitry Svetlov for Game Developer

That’s what I’ll check next time. When design feels “off”, the question isn’t whether the contradiction should be resolved. It’s whether the tension creates meaning and whether contradictory experiences reveal something meaningful about the player, the character, or the world.

If you’ve spotted this same pattern somewhere else (a game, an app, a piece of software) that seemed “inconsistent” on purpose I’d genuinely like to hear about it.

All screenshots and gameplay footage are my own captures from my playthrough of Indika unless a different source is credited.

title: From frictionless to meaningful
text:
From frictionless to meaningful

Inviting friction into design and life

Good design is frictionless, right? When a product seamlessly fits into our lives, when a digital experience is smooth and without problems, that is what we call successful design. It’s when we experience friction with a product that we start to pay attention. A Slack outage. A phone where the user interface makes it hard to find the call button. A shirt that, despite its promise, doesn’t protect against the ice-cold wind. A designer’s goal and dream are to create frictionless experiences that just work.

Designers quickly learn that friction = bad and then we spend most of our time trying to remove friction in order to improve experiences.

However, is this desire for, or obsession with, frictionlessness always a good thing? Can friction actually enrich experiences?

During a recent hike up a mountain in Germany, my friend and designer Molly and I started talking about friction and design. The topic came up as we were struggling to catch our breath with the increasing elevation. Molly explained that:

“We spend so much time making things frictionless, but by making it frictionless we make it forgettable.”

DesignShift: From Frictionless to Meaningful

Molly’s reflection made me consider the many ways that frictionless often means meaningless and the many ways that we can benefit from more friction in our lives.

These are the emerging ways that friction brings meaning to our lives:

  1. Friction creates memorable experiences
  2. Friction invites reflection
  3. Friction invites responsibility
  4. Friction raises awareness
  5. Friction helps us connect with other people
  6. Friction helps us consume less
  7. Friction enables learning
  8. Friction helps us do hard things

1. Friction creates memorable experiences

The first topic I want to explore is the idea that Molly expressed during our hike: “We spend so much time making things frictionless, but by making it frictionless we make it forgettable.”

Think about the most memorable experiences of your life. Chances are, they weren’t the times when everything went smoothly. They were the moments filled with challenge, effort, and yes — friction. The hike where you got lost but discovered a hidden waterfall. The meal you struggled to cook but finally perfected. The project that pushed you to your limits but resulted in work you’re truly proud of.

There’s also what researchers call the effort heuristic. It is our tendency to value things more when we’ve put effort into them. When we struggle through something, overcome obstacles, and finally succeed, the achievement feels more significant. IKEA famously benefits from this with the “IKEA effect” — people value furniture more when they’ve assembled it themselves, despite the frustration of deciphering instruction manuals and searching for missing screws. The friction of assembly creates attachment and memory.

2. Friction invites reflection: Make Me Think

One of the most popular books in design is Don’t Make Me Think by Steve Krug. It’s a practical guide to making websites and digital interfaces easy to use. Krug emphasizes that users should be able to navigate and interact with a site without having to stop and think. He encourages designers to focus on clarity, simplicity, and usability by following familiar design conventions, minimizing distractions, and making key actions obvious.

It’s a book about creating good user experiences, and while it provides a lot of valuable tips for designers, it also creates a false narrative that less friction is always good.

Let’s look at an example from the world of e-commerce. In this space, we often see the strategy of reduced friction as a way for companies to sell more products people might not actually need. On the website KindCommerce created by friend and co-creator Anna Rátkai, she explains how “Companies use buy-now buttons instead of add-to-cart to reduce friction in the checkout and generate more impulse purchases.” Consumers experience frictionlessness. It might feel nice in the moment, but often has long-term consequences. Impulsive decisions often lead to overspending while causing additional harm to our already hurting planet.

Making people think by adding friction can help people stop buying things they don’t really need. It can help them reflect on their actions before taking them.

3. Friction invites responsibility

A lot of designers have good intentions. We want to create work that helps people. We want to make sure that our work does not cause harm. However, caught between compressed timelines and budget cuts, we’re forced to take shortcuts and those shortcuts can have unintended negative consequences. As I was exploring the idea of friction as a catalyst for good, I also started thinking about how we can use friction or moments of pausing in order to hold ourselves accountable.

When I worked at IDEO, we worked on innovation projects that lasted around 12 weeks. We went through the design thinking process in order to create new and innovative solutions for our clients. The process was fast; we worked long nights and weekends in order to have something to present to the clients. There was not a lot of time for reflection. There was not time to stop and say: wait a minute, what are we missing?

In the tech industry, we celebrate speed. “Move fast and break things” was Facebook’s motto for years. But what gets broken in that rush? Often, it’s the careful consideration of consequences. When we optimize for frictionless development processes, we skip the uncomfortable questions: Who might this harm? What are we not considering? Whose voices are missing from this room?

I believe that “Good design is a dance between curiosity AND criticality.” In design thinking, we use the question “how might we” to encourage opportunities through curiosity. As often as we ask “how might we” we also have to ask “at what cost”.

4. Friction raises awareness

If you’ve ever had a Tony’s Chocolonely bar before, you’ve probably noticed that the pieces are different from what you’re used to seeing. Rather than perfectly straight and easy-to-break-off rows, the pieces are uneven. Some are big and others are small. The unevenness makes it hard to break the pieces off. The company has gotten a lot of complaints from customers about the pieces. Most people find them hard to break off. The unevenness creates friction for customers just looking to enjoy a piece of chocolate.

However, there is a story to the friction. In the FAQs on their website, they write:

“To us it doesn’t make sense for chocolate bars to be divided into chunks of equal sizes when there is so much inequality in the chocolate industry! The unevenly sized chunks of our 6oz bars are a palatable way of reminding our choco friends that the profits in the chocolate industry are unfairly divided.”

Today, the majority of cocoa farming is done in West Africa with farmers earning as little as 78 cents per day — well below the World Bank’s extreme poverty line of $1.90 per day. Child labor is a major problem with an estimate of 1.56 million children currently working in cocoa farming.

The uneven pieces represent this inequality and how Tony’s Chocolonely is trying to change this one uneven piece at a time. The friction within the product creates an opportunity for Tony’s to raise awareness and highlight how their product stands for more than taste and form. The friction creates an opportunity to connect with customers. Some might have bought the chocolate just because it tastes good or because of the pretty packaging, but Tony’s is not just looking to sell another chocolate bar. They want to create friction in the industry in order to create systematic change.

5. Friction helps us connect with other people

We live frictionless lives that promise ease, but somehow, loneliness is on the rise.

When I started working on the DesignShifts, I wanted to explore the shift “From convenience to connection.” This topic relates closely to our practices in design, but I also realized that when we talk about frictionless, most of the time we’re also talking about convenience. Our solutions are meant to make life simpler, to optimize experiences. To help us get from A to B quicker. Convenience often equals frictionless.

Kyla Scanlon reflects on how many of our digital experiences provide an escape from the real world which often has a lot of friction. Dating apps, curated social media feeds, instantly translating headphones, and food delivered at the push of a button are easy to turn to when the real world feels challenging.

Optimized, convenient, and frictionless experiences often mean that human connections are removed. Because human interactions increase the likelihood for friction. We have apps that make it easier to order food without any human interactions. This might feel nice in the moment, but it might also lead to increased isolation and disconnection.

The unintended consequences of convenience are that we’re becoming less connected to our communities. The design solutions are making it easy to avoid human interactions.

6. Friction makes us consume less

Two years ago, I decided to stop shopping at Amazon. The convenience of the platform had kept me hooked for a long time, but I also kept seeing stories about their inhumane work conditions, strategies to outprice all independent local bookstores, and the ever-growing wealth of Jeff Bezos. These issues kept nagging me so one day, I decided to stop using their service.

My decision added a lot of friction. When I needed supplies to fix tiles in my bathroom, my free Amazon next-day delivery was replaced with a 20-minute bike ride through the city, 20 minutes of searching a large hardware store with the help of a shop assistant, only to arrive home noticing I’d picked up the wrong color. The experience was quite frustrating and took a lot of time and energy. However, not shopping at Amazon made me aware of all the things I bought “just because.” When I needed something small for my house, I always ended up buying additional things — both to get free shipping, but also because I might need this later. When I stopped using Amazon, I stopped shopping as much. The friction led me to reconsider many purchases. The friction led me to not buy extra things I did not need.

7. Friction enables learning

Many times in my career and life I’ve thought to myself “I wish I could just click a button and I would know all this already.” I often feel this way with my slow-moving German language progress. Wouldn’t it be nice to have a magic button that took us to the finish line right away? Or better yet, would it be better if someone else could do the task for us?

Our brains are wired to remember things that require effort. Cognitive psychology shows us that information processed with more difficulty is often retained better — a phenomenon known as desirable difficulty. When we remove all friction from an experience, we also remove the cognitive engagement that helps us form lasting memories. Yes, sometimes I wish that my German would be perfect already. I wish that I could skip the pain of the process. However, learning isn’t just in service of an end product. Learning is also in service of expansion of minds, hearts, and souls. Learning is in service of stronger connections. Learning is in service of living. When we learn, we expand and that’s what life is about.

A Reflection
Just because we have calculators, doesn’t mean we don’t need to understand math.
Just because we can auto-generate art, doesn’t mean we shouldn’t create a painting.
Just because we can summarize a book in seconds, doesn’t mean it’s not worth reading the full story.
Just because we can buy food at the store, doesn’t mean we shouldn’t learn about how our food is grown.
Just because AI can do a task for us, doesn’t mean it’s not worth learning.
AI might know everything and be able to do everything. Just because we could skip the learning (which is living), doesn’t mean we should.

8. Friction helps us do MORE hard things

I want to end where we started: alongside Molly in the German mountains. During that hike Molly also said that: “When you learn that you can handle some friction, you realize you can handle even more. By always trying to reduce even small amounts of friction, we take away our own power to handle hard things.”

We’ve been removed from pressure. However, frictionless experiences limit our ability to do hard things in the future. Psychologist Michael Inzlicht at the University of Toronto has studied what he calls the “effort paradox”: while humans naturally avoid effort, engaging in challenging activities often leads to a deeper sense of meaning and personal growth. In an episode of the Hidden Brain podcast, Inzlicht explains that effort is inherently meaningful, and activities requiring more exertion paradoxically become more satisfying and purposeful.

When we constantly optimize for ease and eliminate friction from our experiences, we rob ourselves of the capacity to build mental and physical resilience. Like muscles that atrophy without use, our ability to handle difficulty weakens when we never practice it.

This has profound implications for how we design our lives and products. Each time we remove a small friction (autoplay that removes the choice to continue watching, one-click purchasing that bypasses reflection, AI that completes our thoughts before we’ve fully formed them) we’re not just making life easier. We’re also reducing our tolerance for challenge and diminishing our sense of capability.

Snake’s and humans need friction to move forward

I want to take a moment to reflect on this piece that Lilian Marino wrote as the year of the snake started in 2025. In it, she writes “Snakes need friction to move forward. They press against surfaces, grip, and even shift their own scales to generate traction. Without friction, they’re stuck.”

What if we designed friction into our lives in order to create memorable moments, think and reflect, become aware, take responsibility, connect, learn, and do Heard things.

When I think about all the benefits of friction, I also think of it as the path forward. Friction as a path forward fills me with a sense of empowerment. This year, I want to use friction as a tool to move away from ease, speed, and invisibility towards awareness, reflection, and transparency.

Additional Resources

  • LCD Weekly Issue — 029 — Let’s bring friction into design!
  • Steve Selzer: Designing for Friction
  • In 2026, we are friction-maxxing
  • New York Times Opinion on Instagram: “Is online life becoming too easy?”
  • Liminal design: A conceptual framework and three-step approach for developing technology that delivers transcendence and deeper experiences
  • The Costs of Instant Translation

title: The Real Difference Between A $29 Cashmere Sweater And A $295 One
text:
The Real Difference Between A $29 Cashmere Sweater And A $295 One

There is a specific kind of disappointment reserved for cheap cashmere. You buy an “air-conditioned mall” knit thinking you’ve outsmarted the luxury market. It feels deceptively soft on the hanger, but the moment you wear it out into the world, the illusion shatters. After one afternoon, the silhouette sags, the cuffs stretch out, and an aggressive, fuzzy haze of pilling forms along the underarms almost immediately. By wear number three, it’s just embarrassing.

Which begs an obvious shopping question: What actually justifies the leap from a high-street knit to a $295-plus investment piece? Is it just brand prestige, or is there tangible, physical proof woven into the threads?

To find out, I traveled to Northern Italy with luxury knitwear house Falconeri, tracing the journey of a single garment from raw material to finished product. Visiting their yarn mills in Biella and their facility and HQ in Avio, I watched every stage of production unfold. What I discovered is that true cashmere quality isn’t necessarily built in a flash of genius. It’s layered, step by painstaking step, kinda like a good lasagna. Here is what separates run-of-the-mill knits from pieces built to last for years (and how to make sure your investment stays pristine for years to come).

DashDividers_1_500x100

Long Versus Short Fibers

The quality gap begins long before a single thread is spun into yarn. On the factory floor in Biella, the first thing that hit me was the sheer scale of the raw material: massive pallets of fluffy raw Mongolian goat hair arriving straight from the pastures. Holding that raw undercoat in its bulk form before its undergone any industrial processing is like touching wearable cotton candy, without the stickiness. It’s extraordinarily soft, super light, and extremely delicate.

Even if the source is the same, here’s where the budget brands cut costs: They rely on short, thick, leftover fibers (often the sweepings or coarse outer hairs) to whip together their sweaters. Because short fibers don’t have enough length to anchor securely into a yarn, their raw ends stick out. The moment your arms rub against your sides, those loose ends roll into immediate, stubborn pills.

High-tier houses source long, ultrathin fibers from the goat’s undercoat. Long-staple fibers interlock tightly when twisted, creating a smooth, strong yarn that resists surface friction and retains its softness without disintegrating.

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Factories

Seeing the raw fiber was impressive, but the technical yarn-spinning process was where the engineering clicked for me. Falconeri operates an entire factory dedicated exclusively to turning raw fleece into refined yarn. Inside, every batch of fiber is dyed, conditioned with natural oils, rested for a week to balance moisture, and precisely carded or combed. Optical sensors continuously scan the moving threads, automatically cutting out even micro-imperfections before the strands are twisted together. From there, the yarn travels to a second dedicated facility in Avio, where it is transformed into the actual garments.

This isn’t mass assembly. It is high-precision craftsmanship. I watched skilled seamstresses painstakingly hand-link individual threads to state-of-the-art Japanese knitting machines, ensuring seams lie completely flat and never pull or distort over time. When you watch a single garment pass through dozens of hands, sensors, and quality checks, the cost-per-wear makes total sense.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Year-Round Styling

Because high-quality cashmere is naturally thermoregulating, treating it solely as a “winter sweater” is a missed opportunity. Fine-gauge knits belong in your wardrobe rotation 365, 24/7. I put my ultrafine sweater to the test in the scorching summer of Milan, wearing it with my go-to capris and kitten heels. Tying it around your neck is always a smart option, too. It especially comes in handy when the air conditioner is blasting indoors. For cool fall mornings, I plan on letting a thin white T-shirt peek from underneath the V-neckline and wearing it with everything, from jeans to pencil skirts.

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Cashmere Care

The most shocking insight from my conversations with the craftsmen in Milan came down to laundry care. Like most people, I had spent years assuming cashmere was strictly a “dry clean only” situation (probably because of the nightmare experiences I’ve had in the past with synthetic hybrids). The artisans laughed at that idea because dry cleaning uses harsh chemicals that strip the fiber’s natral oils over time. Their actual directive? Cashmere loves water. You can safely wash your knits in a standard washing machine provided you use a low-tumble, delicate cycle with cold water and gentle detergent. Low friction is the goal.

Next you’ll want to get ahead of pilling and comb your sweater before it starts. The craftsman showed me how running a fine cashmere comb lightly over friction points catches stray strands before they form those dense pills.

Lastly, remember that gravity is the enemy. Heavy hangers stretch the shoulder seams and ruin the necklines on structured knits. So never hang them. Instead, lay them flat to dry or store them folded.

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Investment Pieces

If you’re ready to build a knitwear collection that actually lasts, skip the fast-fashion rack and focus on versatile, long-fiber staples. You aren’t just paying for a label when you upgrade your knitwear. You are paying for a piece of sartorial joy that holds its shape, honors Italian craftsmanship, and gets softer every time it touches water. Skip the $29 sweaters that end up in the donation bin by November, and invest in a knit that will earn its keep for years and years to come.

title: Here’s Everything We Know About Children Of Blood and Bone — & Its Controversy
text:
Here’s Everything We Know About Children Of Blood and Bone — & Its Controversy

The Children of Blood and Bone controversy may not be coming to an end anytime soon. After the trailer for the Paramount Pictures film adaptation of the bestselling novel dropped on Tuesday, author Tomi Adeyemi doubled down on her decision to distance herself from the project. She shared in a TikTok video that working on the film was “the worst thing I have ever had to live through” that resulted in her “hyperventilating” to the point where she had to leave the set.

“There are many witnesses, so it’s not really a secret,” the Nigerian-American author said in the video. “I came back to America and suffered such severe somatic pain and so many panic attacks. I knew it was so bad that I would never ever be able to watch this film, and I made peace with that.”

@tomi.adeyemi #childrenofbloodandbone ♬ original sound – tomi adeyemi

Fans are wondering what actually happened for Adeyemi to entirely cut ties. Calling this adaptation highly anticipated would be an understatement. The film, shot in IMAX, projected to be a big screen blockbuster that could rival the impact of The Hunger Games and has been compared to the expansive world of Harry Potter. With a star-studded cast, and direction by Gina Prince-Bythewood, Children of Blood and Bone could open new doors in the fantasy film genre when it hits theaters January 15, 2027. 

Though Adeyemi nor the filmmakers have given much detail about what happened behind the scenes, some fans are wondering what the controversy means for the project. Though Adeyemi has announced herself that she will not be seeing the adaptation of her novel, she has not sent a call-to-action for her fans to also abstain from the film. In fact, in response to a comment on a since-deleted TikTok video, the 32-year old said “I do not mind anyone going to watch the film.” She continued, “I wrote this for us. I fought for us. I’m just laying down my sword and officially separating my name because I can’t keep being hurt and attacked behind the scenes.”

Audiences have mixed feelings about the film. Some have expressed that they, too, will be sitting this one out to support Adeyemi, while others feel like the roles Amandla Stenberg and other cast members hold should’ve been for Nigerian actors. Still, some fans’ support for the film hasn’t wavered, especially considering the unfair standards Black filmmakers face when studios look at box office numbers.

This is an unfortunate controversy. Children of Blood and Bone has had a generational impact as a YA novel that has broken barriers for how big fantasy that centers Black characters can be. And though it is not the first text based in Africa that uses magic, spirituality and cultural tradition to weave together a stunningly resonant story, it is the first of its kind to get the massive budgeting and Hollywood hype typically reserved for films with white-dominant casting. It’s expected to become one of the biggest fantasy features next year. Many worry that if this film doesn’t meet the mark at the box office, it may be a long time before another Black writer or director — let alone a Black woman — gets to showcase a fantastical world at this level. 

We may not know the root cause of the controversy but here’s a timeline of how we got here.

March 6, 2018: Tomi Adeyemi publishes Children of Blood and Bone

At 24, Tomi Adeyemi released Children of Blood and Bone, the first of three books in her groundbreaking Legacy of Orïsha series. The YA novel is set in a fictional African nation where protagonist Zélie Adebola sets out to bring magic back to the people of her kingdom who have been stripped of their power by an oppressive regime. Published by Henry Holt Books for Young Readers, Adeyemi received a historic book deal that included preemptive filmmaking rights which sold to Fox 2000 Pictures. Children of Blood and Bone debuted at No. 1 on New York Times’ Bestsellers List and spent over 120 weeks in the rankings. The Nigerian-American author also has earned several literary awards and was named on the Time 100 list in 2019 and 2020. 

January 2022: Adeyemi lands a seven-figure deal with Paramount Pictures 

The film was initially developed under George Lucas’ Lucasfilm with This Is Us writer Kay Oyegun penning the script and Rick Famuyiwa directing. After Disney’s acquisition of 20th Century Fox, Lucasfilm let the rights on the film lapse. A major bidding war ensued between studios, including Universal, Amazon and Netflix. Paramount Pictures came out victorious, obtaining the rights to the Children of Blood and Bone trilogy, which also includes Children of Virtue and Vengeance (December 2019) and Children of Anguish and Anarchy (June 2024). When first announced, Deadline reported that her deal included a seven-figure screenwriting guarantee, creative approvals for the author as executive producer and a guaranteed theatrical release.

“Paramount’s passion and enthusiasm to bring this story to life has been incredible,” Adeyemi told the trade outlet at the time. “We are all so excited for this new chapter and are already hard at work.”

December 14, 2023: Gina Prince-Bythewood announced as director

Prince-Bythewood entered the project as its new director. She also co-wrote the script with Adeyemi with her husband, Reggie Rock Bythewood, serving as an executive producer. The Love & Basketball director said that she was approached to take the helm of Children of Blood and Bone three times over the course of seven years, noting that the timing wasn’t right the first two times. When she was approached the third time, she had The Woman King and The Old Guard under her belt. She noted that those films gave her the technical and emotional readiness to tell the story.

“I couldn’t say no,” she told the Los Angeles Times. “It was something even bigger in a space that we hadn’t got to see ourselves in, which is fantasy and big, epic fantasy.”

Since being named director, both Prince-Bythewood and Adeyemi have discussed their alignment on record. In June 2024, Adeyemi sang the director’s praises in an interview with Elle. “What Gina does so well is tell these deep, complex stories of women who look like us front and center, with incredible action set pieces, incredible cinematography,” she said. “It feels divine. It feels bigger than [just] making this project. We’re really in sync.” 

This month, Prince-Bythewood told Essence that co-signing on the film with Adeyemi “was everything.” She said they were aligned through scripting, artwork and more. “And that’s inspiring as a director because again, we’re here because of something that came from her and we want to honor that,” the director said.

January 22, 2025: The principal cast draws initial criticism

Thuso Mbedu, Damson Idris and Amandla Stenberg lead this ensemble cast, which also includes Viola Davis, Regina King, Idris Elba, Cynthia Erivo, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Zackary Momoh, Tosin Cole and Lashana Lynch. A predominantly Black cast with major star power wasn’t enough to quell audiences’ concerns over certain casting choices, however. Readers called out colorism after Stenberg was announced as one of the main protagonists, who is described as having “dark copper skin” and contends with colorism and fatphobia in the book. Folks also took issue with a lack of Nigerian representation, pointing to the novel’s Yoruba roots.

Stenberg, who also received similar backlash for playing the role of Starr Carter in The Hate U Give, responded to the criticism in a since-deleted TikTok video posted on February 2025, noting that being “at odds with my own community,” felt more painful than the racism she received from being cast in the Star Wars universe.

The actor also acknowledged how colorism plays out in the industry and said that she only felt comfortable going after the role after meeting with Adeyemi and getting her blessing. 

“I had the opportunity to meet Tomi, the novelist, for the first time … And she goes, ‘Amandla, I want you to know that when you were a little girl and you were cast as Rue in The Hunger Games, and people said that Rue’s death wouldn’t be as sad because you’re a Black girl—that inspired me to write this series so that Black girls like you and Black girls of all shades could have a story written about them,’” Stenberg said. “We started crying, and I said to myself, ‘God wants me here.’”

During a June 2025 interview, podcaster Zethu Gqola asked Adeyemi about the criticism around the actor’s casting, to which the author responded that she “understand[s] when people are frustrated.” She also addressed the concerns over Nigerian representation.

“If you need me to be a punching bag, I get it because just like you, I’ve been hurt so many times by this industry and the feeling of being erased by it.” She added, “If you feel brokenhearted by this, I don’t think you’ll feel like that when you’re sitting in the theaters. I promise you, this world is so beautiful and we’re all in it and that’s so beautiful to me.”

During the interview, Adeyemi also noted that the film features Nigerian actors selected from the casting call filmmakers held across the West African country. 

The film also features Saniyya Sidney, Diaana Babnicova, Bukky Bakray, Ayra Starr, Pamilerin Afolake Ayodeji, Shamz Garuba, Kola Bodunde and Tèmítópé Fágbénlé.

July 4, 2026: Adeyemi begins distancing herself from the film

The author posted a cryptic TikTok video stating that she would not be watching the film. “There is a reason I will not post anything about the adaptation of my work. That’s all,” she wrote in a screenshotted conversation. The video has since been deleted. The post also included screenshots of a conversation between herself and Stenberg stemming from a text exchange in February 2025, around the time Stenberg posted their response to the casting criticism. 

“Do not ever use my name in an interview or video again. Do not text me. Do not call me,” the message read, according to the Los Angeles Times. Adeyemi also appeared to have blocked Stenberg.

Adeyemi was also noticeably absent from a special sneak peak screening at CinemaCon in April 2026.

July 27, 2026: The Children of Blood and Bone trailer drops

At a trailer premiere screening in Brooklyn on Monday, Prince-Bythewood said the film is “beautifully inspired by Nigeria and also inclusive of the whole diaspora. We wanted all of us to be able to see ourselves within this, just our complete and utter humanity, all the beautiful hues.”

July 29, 2026 Adeyemi recalls the day she left set hyperventilating

The day after Paramount released the film’s first trailer, Ayedemi shared a five-minute long TikTok discussing an undisclosed traumatic experience she had which prompted her to leave the “set of my own film adaptation, hyperventilating and sobbing.” Though she doesn’t go into much detail, she claims that she continued to be “antagonised” even after her departure. The author stated that if she didn’t ring the alarm, things would only get worse. 

She stated that she “suffered such severe somatic pain and so many panic attacks,” upon returning from Cape Town to America after filming. “I knew it was so bad that I would never ever be able to watch this film, and I made peace with that,” she said. 

What’s next?

We’re still six months away from this film’s release. Whether audiences find out what the controversy is centered on remains to be seen, especially considering the filmmakers and studio have yet to comment. It’s also too early to say whether or not Children of Virtue and Vengeance and Children of Anguish and Anarchy will also get screen adaptations.

Adeyemi was also set to make a cameo in the film. With her current stance on the film, it’s likely her appearance will not make the final cut. Her representatives told People that her current focus is promoting The Siren, her forthcoming novel which releases in September.

We’ll update this article with more details as the story unfolds…

title: How Influencer Toni Bravo became the CEO of Blush
text:
How Influencer Toni Bravo became the CEO of Blush

Toni Bravo is the CEO of Blush and an influencer powerhouse. Based in Los Angeles, the California native has built a loyal community well into the millions because of her impeccable taste and advocacy for inclusivity in the beauty industry. Toni joined host Brooke DeVard on the Naked Beauty Podcast to talk about her life before a viral blush try-on video changed everything. She shared what it was like to grow up as a fraternal twin in the sunny and very diverse Long Beach. They talk about her early forays into filming and editing herself and her family at just nine years old, simply for the love of storytelling. She detailed how influential the women in her life were to shaping the way she saw the beauty in herself and the world around her. It’s precisely this love of telling intimate stories that have shaped her POV into the one beloved by so many.

Toni doesn’t hold back when it comes to the realities of being a successful and full-time content creator, especially when advocating for dark-skinned Black women’s access to high-quality beauty. It was very interesting to learn how she maintains strong brand relationships without compromising the truth about product efficacy. She details the commitment and self-trust one has to have to succeed, because your point of view is everything. During their conversation, Toni talked about her interest in product development and why she isn’t limiting herself in anything. Toni also blessed the podcast with a quick tour of her favorite products, from skincare, to haircare, and of course blush! They covered her recent Architectural Digest feature and the intentional design choices that went into making her home, hers.

title: How Aora Beauty Founder Nour Tayara Made Sustainability Beautiful
text:
How Aora Beauty Founder Nour Tayara Made Sustainability Beautiful

Nour Tayara joins the Naked Beauty Podcast to talk about his innovative and 100% plastic-free beauty brand, AORA. During the conversation with host Brooke DeVard, he shared how he found his place in Lebanon’s underground queer scene and shaped his life’s motto to be kind and engaging to everyone, wherever you are. They talk about how Nour supplemented his scholarship by taking guerrilla marketing jobs and how they changed his mind about his electrical engineering major. Nour explains how an incredibly high test score landed him an internship and ultimately a full-time role at L’Oréal, where he worked for 13 years.

As Nour’s role and responsibilities evolved, he learned more about the waste and overconsumption plaguing the industry. Always prepared to innovate, he pitched a plastic-free brand to his management, which was promptly rejected. While reeling from a series of difficult events, Nour shared that a four-month break in Mexico City ultimately led him to his co-founder. The pair were aligned on building a brand that celebrates Mexican culture and is 100% plastic-free. Join them for an incredible conversation about what happens when you stay open to possibilities for your future and your principles are immovable. Nour details what it means to him to bring color to the clean beauty movement, why Mexico has always been a lifeline, and what it feels like to disrupt an industry.

title: Is Spider-Man: Brand New Day Worth Watching? Our Honest Review
text:
Is Spider-Man: Brand New Day Worth Watching? Our Honest Review

Zendaya and Tom Holland have been making waves with their Spider-Man: Brand New Day press tour, but is the film worth watching? The anticipated sequel to Spider-Man: No Way Home has just hit theaters, and it’s a more grounded, serious look at Spider-Man’s life as he attempts to live life in solitude. The film has received an overwhelmingly positive response from critics, with a solid score of 91% on Rotten Tomatoes.

It’s easy to dismiss Spider-Man: No Way Home as a superhero film that’s all about action and big set pieces, but there’s a deep look into what makes you unique, how connection and relationships are so important, and it will make you want to call your best friend.

Below, entertainment writers Angeline Barion, Bernice Corral and Rachel Choy examine what makes Spider-Man: No Way Home so emotional, the acting performances from Sadie Sink, Zendaya and Tom Holland, and how many tissues they went through. Spoilers below.

Rachel Choy: How excited were you for this movie?!

Bernice Corral: Literally my most anticipated movie of the year. From Sony.

Angeline Barion: I’m not usually openly expressive about how much of a fan I am about things, except for minions. So this coming out around the same time meant I had an out of body experience. I think I almost blew up, like spontaneously combusted. That’s the level of excitement.

RC: I want to know the level of tissues. How many tissues did you use?

AB: I bought a packet of 60 Kleenex tissues, and I think that collectively between three of us sitting in the same row as really big Spider-Man fans, I think we got through 20, and we had like a whole plastic cup full.

RC: Let’s talk about the performances to begin with. What did you think of Tom Holland?

BC: I mean he’s great, but did he need to be topless that much?

RC: Yeah, he didn’t need to be in his undies. But also, he did. Wait, guys, can we talk about the moment he got his organic web?

AB: That was a bit red hot.

RC: It was like jizz. It was splurting, and I was like, did we need such a close up?

AB: But also, I was just thinking about the passage of how much time had passed from when he passed out to when he woke up in that web. He really put his body on the line in this particular movie, and I thought his performance was amazing.

RC: The yearning!

AB: You could see it in his eyes, and he was just stoic. He was just looking for MJ the whole time.

RC: But also low-key stalkerish because she doesn’t know who he is!

BC: Well, yeah. When he showed up to her apartment, I was like, that’s trespassing.

RC: I was like boy, just read her the letter! Don’t do this, please. And what did you think of newcomer Sadie Sink?

BC: I just love her. I watched her in Stranger Things, she’s great.

RC: She was so good as Jean Grey, and I love X-Men. I’m not the hugest Marvel girl. I dropped off a little bit, but I’ve watched all the old X-Men films and all the Spider-Man ones. The depth and emotion in her, with her backstory and how they were treated like animals, there’s a lot to unpack there. Very similar to how you’re treated in our world if you’re different.

AB: I’ve never watched any of her stuff before, so this is the first time I’ve ever encountered Sadie. I think I was so drawn to her because she has quite an expressive forehead and eyes. The top section of her face is quite expressive.

RC: Also, her power was so cool. You could physically see her jumping from person to person. It was such a big jerk.

AB: The extras were so good! They just took it full force, and the way they were moving around, I was like, this could actually happen in real life and you wouldn’t notice. So if any telepaths are out there, some of our brains are rot.

BC: You could tell when she was possessing them and how they were able to capture it. Yeah, wow, your IMDB is gonna be crazy after this.

RC: What did you think about Zendaya, our MJ?

BC: One of the wigs she was wearing wasn’t my fave.

AB: It was the second one.

BC: You’re wearing a wig.

RC: Wigs aside, the scene where she was possessed by Jean Grey and Peter Parker thought his MJ remembered him?! You knew it was coming. I was screaming.

BC: The switch she was able to do between MJ and then possessed by Jean.

AB: I’m floored by her. I have no words to describe or encapsulate how well she played that, and keeping it a secret as well. I think that was really hard, especially Tom being her actual husband. I think that that plays such a big part of it. But damn, that twist in the, I’m not gonna say it outright, but the twist in The Punisher’s house was devastating.

RC: It adds such a human quality to it because because there’s a lot of big scenes and set pieces, but I feel like the small scenes actually had the most impact.

BC: I feel like with her character MJ, it’s been very surface level for the past movies, but then this one we’re able to see her depth. People didn’t take her seriously as an actor until this year.

RC: She wasn’t in the first one very much, and they were so little and young, so now there’s all the years of trauma growing up. So there’s that scene in the Punisher’s house, but there was also the Lego scene.

BC: Don’t talk to me about that.

AB: No, no, no, no!

BC: It’s a movie about trauma.

AB: I love that they called back to her first performance though, with the drawing and Lego. I think that that was really special because it really ties their friendship together. Despite obviously having lost it and then coming back together, it’s the small things. You can go a length of time without talking to a person or seeing a person, but there’s always something that ties you together. And I think they really nailed how that chemistry works between the three of them in that Lego scene.

BC: It didn’t feel forced.

AB: They’re just hanging out. I feel like if they were just hanging out at someone’s house, that’s literally what they would do.

RC: The other big plot point is the inhibitor. How much of your DNA can you change before you become a completely different person?

AB: I thought that’s how they were going to write the Hulk out of the MCU, because he becomes a monster, and all that. But I think that’s such a side thought. This whole theme was great because it leans into the whole being yourself, showing your true colors to your friends, being open and honest and authentic, and how you don’t have to walk through things alone, even when they’re difficult. And even when Jean broke her inhibitor, and that’s how she was able to have the release. I think it really also feeds into that like plotline, that theme, that narrative.

RC: And it’s exhausting to try to be something that you’re not. Loneliness is such a big theme as well. He’s trying to do everything perfectly, but his body just says no.

BC: Reach out when you need to.

RC: Everyone needs connection, whether it’s relationships or friendships. It’s so important. The one critique I had was there were the cameos from the other MCU characters. Sometimes you just want more from the character that’s the title character. I know they need the crossover so it can set up the next Avengers. But I wanted more of Spider-Man.

AB: Him and Ned. I think that we, especially in this particular press tour, we’re so focused on like Tom’s and Zendaya. Their relationship is so beautiful and admirable, but I think that this film really leans on Peter and Ned as well, and their connection to each other. I wish we got to see more of that because, the guy in the chair is such an iconic part of the franchise for for Tom Holland’s Spider-Man. And with Ned’s aura blow up, he just had an extreme amount of confidence, but at the same time, he was still that little nerdy boy on the inside. I wish that we got to see more of him playing that part out.

RC: He’s such a genuine, friendly character. There’s nothing sinister, he’s just wholesome. I want more of that.

AB: Can they make side movies?

BC: Shorts, like Ned’s Side Quest!

RC: Where does it rank out of Tom Holland’s Spider-Man films?

BC: I will say No Way Home, I do love that… but I love Homecoming. This is genuinely really hard. I will say I love how they brought it back to street level with this one and it was grounded in reality. It wasn’t like a portal opens up.

RC: I think this is why I love this one the most.

BC: He’s just a little guy!

RC: I quite liked how depressed he was. Because then he’ll have to get happy. He’s at rock bottom, so he can only get better… we hope.

AB: Him being street level, that is so great.

BC: That is the core of what Spider-Man is.

AB: I don’t think it sensationalizes a multiverse and all of these infinite possibilities. I think it just focuses on the one possibility that sometimes things just don’t work out, and you have to find your way to to deal with it. Things that you thought were gonna be forever fall apart, but it just focuses on you doing the simple things, and I think that’s what is great about Spider-Man, and I think that’s what so many people love about Spider-Man.

RC: Is it worth watching?

AB: I think if you are a Spider-Man fan, I think you’ll be happy.

RC: If you’re a casual fan or a bit neutral?

AB: I think the good thing with Spider-Man is it can stand on its own. You don’t have to watch the other Marvel movies in order to understand it. I think that this one feels like it can create its own line. Obviously it connects to the MCU, but this can standalone. It lives within like the same universe as Homecoming and Far From Home.

I think it does it justice, and I think that everyone should watch it. Doesn’t matter if you’re a Spider-Man fan or you’re not a Spider-Man fan. Even if you’re just feeling like you’re going through something and you don’t have people around you, and that’s literally that’s that’s what it is. It makes me emotional because I was sitting next to my best friend, and we sometimes go periods of time where we don’t talk to each other.

RC: You have that connection.

AB: That drawing scene, she draws in the same style. So it was very emotional.

RC: I feel like that you have those friendships that you can go for years being apart. I’ve lived so many places and overseas for years. But my best friend since I was 14, every time I see her, it’s like nothing’s changed. And I feel like if I even if I forgot my memories and connected with her, I feel like she’s in my soul. You just know each other. You just get it.

AB: It’s part of your DNA.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is in theaters now.
